item.title: NetNut Disruption, Citrix Bleed 2 Ransomware, and Snowflake SaaS Credential Abuse
AI Agent Prompt Injection, Adobe ColdFusion RCE Paths, and Microsoft 365 ConsentFix Hijacking
ToddyCat Umbrij Hits Gmail; CVE-2026-20230 and CVE-2026-45659 Exploited
JADEPUFFER Langflow RCE, FortiBleed Ransomware Access, and ChocoPoC Fake PoCs
Medtronic Notifies Customers After ShinyHunters Breach Exposes Personal and Health Data
CVE-2026-45659 SharePoint, Cisco Unified CM Exploits, JADEPUFFER AI Ransomware, FortiBleed
item.content:encoded:
ShinyHunters & Rockstar: Snowflake Data Breach Leads to Compromise | Mitiga — Must Read

ShinyHunters allegedly compromised Rockstar by stealing service account tokens from third-party analytics provider Anodot and using that trusted access to exfiltrate Snowflake data. The key lesson is that supply chain attacks often look like legitimate logins, so organizations must monitor service accounts and integration behavior for anomalies.

  • ShinyHunters breached Rockstar Games by first compromising Anodot, a SaaS analytics provider with authenticated access to customer Snowflake environments.
  • The attackers stole service account tokens, used them to log in as legitimate users, and exfiltrated 78.6 million records containing financial data and player spending metrics.
  • The article states that no vulnerability in Snowflake itself was exploited.
  • Anodot’s public status page showed a broad outage on April 4, 2026, affecting all data collectors, including Snowflake, S3, and Kinesis.
  • The article recommends checking whether an organization uses Anodot, reviewing known infrastructure indicators such as Mullvad and Tor nodes, and baselining service account activity.

CISA: Microsoft SharePoint RCE flaw now actively exploited — Must Read

CISA says attackers are now actively exploiting CVE-2026-45659, a Microsoft SharePoint remote code execution flaw that lets low-privileged authenticated users run code on vulnerable servers. Federal agencies have been ordered to patch by Saturday, and exposed SharePoint servers should be updated urgently.

  • CISA warned that attackers have begun exploiting CVE-2026-45659, a high-severity Microsoft SharePoint remote code execution vulnerability.
  • Microsoft says the flaw stems from deserialization of untrusted data and allows an authenticated attacker with minimum Site Member permissions to execute code remotely on SharePoint Server without user interaction.
  • Microsoft released security updates for SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016, SharePoint Server 2019, and SharePoint Server Subscription Edition on May 21 after the CVE was accidentally omitted from the May 2026 Security Updates.
  • CISA added CVE-2026-45659 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and ordered Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to secure their servers by Saturday under Binding Operational Directive 26-04.
  • Shadowserver is tracking over 10,000 SharePoint servers exposed online, but the article says there is no information on how many have been secured against ongoing CVE-2026-45659 attacks.

AI Agent Exploits Langflow RCE to Automate Database Ransomware Attack — Must Read

Sysdig says an AI agent dubbed JADEPUFFER autonomously exploited an unpatched Langflow RCE, stole credentials, pivoted through exposed services, and destroyed a production database in a ransomware-style extortion attempt. The key lesson is that neglected internet-facing AI tools, config stores, and databases are now easy targets for automated agents chaining old vulnerabilities at scale.

  • Sysdig says it found what it believes is the first ransomware attack run from start to finish by an AI agent, which it calls JADEPUFFER.
  • JADEPUFFER exploited CVE-2025-3248, a missing-authentication flaw in Langflow that allows unauthenticated remote Python code execution on reachable servers.
  • After gaining access, the agent searched for API keys, cloud credentials, crypto wallet keys, and database logins, and it also accessed a MinIO server that still used the default minioadmin:minioadmin login.
  • The agent pivoted to an internet-facing MySQL and Nacos server, logged into the database as root, took over Nacos using CVE-2021-29441 and a default signing key, and created its own admin account.
  • The agent encrypted 1,342 Nacos settings, dropped the original tables, deleted whole databases, and left a ransom note, but Sysdig says the encryption key was never saved or sent anywhere.

FortiBleed Credential Theft Linked to INC and Lynx Ransomware Operations — Must Read

SOCRadar linked the FortiBleed credential-theft campaign to INC and Lynx ransomware operations, showing stolen FortiGate admin access is being used for follow-on ransomware attacks. The campaign reportedly scanned thousands of FortiGate portals, compromised hundreds of targets, and led to at least 12 ransomware deployments.

  • SOCRadar attributed the FortiBleed campaign to INC and Lynx ransomware operations after finding an operator tied to FortiBleed infrastructure actively working negotiation panels for both groups.
  • SOCRadar tracked scanning activity against about 11,250 FortiGate portals in more than 150 countries, with confirmed admin-level access on 409 targets and full attack chain completion on 354 of them.
  • At least 12 ransomware deployments have resulted from the FortiBleed access, encrypting hundreds of endpoints across affected organizations.
  • The campaign involved scanning exposed Fortinet devices, trying known credential combinations, and deploying custom packet sniffers to passively collect credentials and other authentication data from network traffic.
  • SOCRadar said tooling, logs, and working hours indicate a Russian-speaking threat actor likely operating as an initial access broker, with much of the targeting focused on manufacturing, technology, and logistics sectors in Latin America and the Asia Pacific regions.

Cisco finally confirms attackers exploiting Unified CM flaw — Must Read

Cisco confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-20230, a Unified CM server-side request forgery flaw with public exploit code. Customers should upgrade to fixed releases immediately or disable the vulnerable WebDialer service until patched.

  • Cisco confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-20230, a Unified Communications Manager vulnerability patched in early June.
  • CVE-2026-20230 can be exploited remotely by unauthenticated attackers in low-complexity server-side request forgery attacks using crafted HTTP requests.
  • Defused reported on June 22 that attackers had begun exploiting the flaw with properly constructed file:// payloads to create files on targeted devices.
  • Cisco urged customers to upgrade to fixed Cisco Unified CM releases and advised those who cannot immediately patch to disable the vulnerable WebDialer service.
  • Shadowserver is tracking over 200 Cisco Unified CM instances exposed online, mostly in Asia and North America.

Ransomware Groups Turn to Citrix Bleed 2, BYOVD, and Supply Chain Credentials — Must Read

Ransomware groups are increasingly combining Citrix Bleed 2 exploitation, stolen or weak credentials, legitimate remote management tools, BYOVD techniques, and supply-chain-derived access to break into networks, evade defenses, and deploy ransomware. The activity highlights a shift toward more industrialized, credential-driven ransomware operations involving groups such as Anubis, The Gentlemen, VECT, and TeamPCP.

  • Anubis ransomware affiliates have exploited the Citrix Bleed 2 vulnerability, CVE-2025-5777, and used valid VPN credentials to gain initial access to victim environments.
  • Anubis intrusions involved legitimate remote management tools such as ScreenConnect, Zoho Assist, MeshAgent, Remotely, UltraVNC, and Total Software Deployment, along with RDP, PsExec, cloudflared, and data transfer tools including S3 Browser, rclone, s5cmd, WinSCP, and PuTTY.
  • The Gentlemen ransomware-as-a-service group used known vulnerabilities, stolen or weak credentials, a Go-based backdoor, and a BYOVD technique involving the ktapi.sys driver to bypass Windows security protections and kill protected security processes.
  • Sophos reported that VECT and TeamPCP formed a partnership to combine supply chain attack-driven credential theft with ransomware deployment across organizations compromised in the Trivy and LiteLLM supply chain attacks.
  • Recent analyses found that VECT contains implementation flaws that permanently destroy files larger than 128 KB rather than encrypting them, while TeamPCP claimed it had never used VECT's encryptor in attacks.

Medtronic notifies customers impacted by ShinyHunters data breach — Must Read

Medtronic is notifying customers after ShinyHunters accessed corporate IT systems and exposed personal and health-related data, potentially including names, contact details, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, and health information. The company says its medical devices were not affected and that the stolen data has not been posted online.

  • Medtronic is notifying affected customers about a data breach that exposed personal data to an unauthorized third party.
  • Medtronic said it detected unusual activity on certain corporate IT systems on April 15, 2026, and an investigation found unauthorized access from April 13 to April 19, 2026.
  • The exposed data may include full names, contact information, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, and health-related information.
  • The ShinyHunters group claimed it held 9 million Medtronic records and listed Medtronic on its dark web extortion portal on April 18 before later removing the entry.
  • Medtronic said the stolen data was not exposed online and that its medical devices remain safe to use and were not affected by the incident.

It’s 37oC, And All We Can Think About Is ColdFusion (Adobe ColdFusion Security Bulletin APSB26-68 CVE Bonanza) — Should Read

Adobe patched a large set of ColdFusion vulnerabilities, including RDS file operations that could allow unauthenticated arbitrary file read/write and remote code execution when RDS is enabled with authentication disabled. Additional CKEditor file manager flaws could also allow path traversal-based uploads or directory listing when the feature is explicitly enabled.

  • Adobe’s June 30 security advisory APSB26-68 addressed multiple vulnerabilities affecting ColdFusion 2025 Update 9 and below and ColdFusion 2023 Update 20 and below.
  • The researchers found that ColdFusion’s Remote Development Services FILEIO functionality could allow arbitrary file read and write when RDS is enabled and authentication is disabled.
  • The article states that the FILEIO write capability could be used to place a ColdFusion file in the web root and achieve remote code execution.
  • The patch changed RDS file handling to use canonical path resolution through RdsFileSecurity, adding checks intended to reject null bytes and parent directory traversal sequences.
  • The researchers also identified path traversal issues in the CKEditor file manager upload and directory listing functionality, while noting that file uploads are disabled by default.

ToddyCat-Linked Umbrij Malware Abuses OAuth to Access Gmail via Google API — Should Read

Kaspersky says the ToddyCat APT is using a new tool called Umbrij to hijack active Gmail sessions in Chrome or Edge, abuse OAuth via Google APIs, and gain covert access to corporate email. Organizations should review and revoke suspicious Google Workspace Migration/Sync for Microsoft Outlook app permissions if they are not legitimately used.

  • Kaspersky attributed a new malware called Umbrij to the ToddyCat threat actor, saying it is designed to access victims’ Gmail correspondence through the Google API.
  • Umbrij abuses an active Gmail session in Chromium-based browsers by launching the browser in headless mode, connecting through a remote debugging port, and obtaining an OAuth authorization code.
  • The malware was discovered during a threat hunting operation in which a scheduled task impersonating Kaspersky software launched a digitally signed file that used DLL side-loading to run the Umbrij DLL.
  • Kaspersky said Umbrij can target Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge, copy browser profile data into BackupFiles folders, and use Puppeteer to interact with the browser and grant permissions to a Google migration-related application.
  • Kaspersky advised organizations to review Google account application connections for “Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook” or “Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook” and revoke access if those applications are not used.

Alleged Scattered Spider hacker extradited to the United States — Should Read

A 19-year-old dual U.S.-Estonian citizen accused of being a Scattered Spider member has been extradited to the United States after his arrest in Finland. Prosecutors allege he helped breach major companies through social engineering and extortion schemes that caused millions in losses.

  • A 19-year-old dual United States and Estonian citizen, Peter Stokes, has been extradited to the United States to face charges alleging he was a member of the Scattered Spider hacking collective.
  • Stokes was arrested in Finland on April 10 while attempting to board a flight to Japan and is accused of helping extort millions of dollars from multiple high-profile companies worldwide.
  • Court documents allege Stokes was involved in at least four Scattered Spider breaches, including a March 2023 hack of an online communication platform and a May 2025 breach of an unnamed multibillion-dollar luxury item retailer.
  • In the luxury retailer incident, hackers allegedly posed as employees when calling the IT helpdesk to reset credentials, demanded an $8 million ransom, and caused the company over $2 million in disruption and remediation costs after it refused to pay.
  • The Justice Department said Scattered Spider has been involved in over 100 network intrusions, resulting in more than $100 million in ransom payments and millions more in victim damages.

New ChocoPoC RAT Targets Vulnerability Researchers via Fake PoC Exploit Repos — Should Read

Attackers are targeting vulnerability researchers with fake GitHub PoC exploit repositories that pull malicious Python dependencies, installing the ChocoPoC RAT to steal credentials, browser data, files, and provide remote shell access. Researchers should avoid running untrusted PoCs, inspect dependency chains, and rebuild/rotate credentials if packages like frint, skytext, slogsec, or logcrypt.cryptography were installed.

  • Attackers are distributing the ChocoPoC data-stealing remote access trojan through fake Python proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub that claim to exploit high-profile CVEs.
  • The visible proof-of-concept code appears clean because the malware is hidden in a Python dependency chain involving the frint and skytext packages.
  • ChocoPoC steals saved passwords, browser cookies, autofill data, browsing history, files, shell history, network settings, and process lists, and it can give attackers shell access to the victim’s machine.
  • YesWeHack and Sekoia found at least seven fake proof-of-concept repositories, and the skytext package alone had about 2,400 downloads, mostly on Linux.
  • Researchers advised checking systems for frint, skytext, slogsec, and logcrypt.cryptography, and rotating credentials and rebuilding hosts if any of them were run.

Google Disrupts NetNut Residential Proxy Network Spanning 2 Million Home Devices — Should Read

Google, working with the FBI, Lumen, and others, says it has significantly degraded NetNut/Popa, a residential proxy network that used millions of home devices such as smart TVs and streaming boxes to relay other people’s traffic. The main risk for consumers is that hidden or poorly disclosed bandwidth-sharing apps can turn their internet connection into an exit node for criminals and other threat actors.

  • Google’s Threat Intelligence Group said it worked with the FBI, Lumen, and others to significantly degrade NetNut, also tracked as Popa, reducing its pool of usable devices by millions.
  • Google identifies NetNut as a residential proxy network spread across at least 2 million home devices worldwide, including smart TVs and streaming boxes.
  • In one week in June, Google counted 316 distinct threat clusters using suspected NetNut exit nodes, including cybercriminal and espionage groups conducting password-guessing attacks.
  • Researchers at Qurium, Synthient, Nokia Deepfield, and Spur tied Popa to NetNut, which is owned by the publicly traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies.
  • Google said the disruption is degradation rather than a kill because NetNut uses reseller relationships and similar networks can buy capacity from rivals or resurface under other brands.

Roblox, Minecraft, and the Insidious Internet for Children — Should Read

Censys research found a large, fast-changing ecosystem of Roblox and Minecraft offerwall scams and phishing sites targeting children, with at least 437 Roblox reward sites and hundreds of spoofing domains. The key takeaway is that defenders cannot rely on threat feeds alone and need content, hostname, and infrastructure fingerprinting to detect and disrupt this abuse.

  • Censys research found 437 web properties matching a Roblox offerwall reward-site fingerprint in a June 2026 snapshot.
  • The Roblox offerwall sites commonly promise Robux or gift cards in exchange for tasks such as surveys, app installs, watching videos, or completing offers.
  • Censys found that many Roblox phishing domains impersonate Roblox, Bloxlink, or RoVer, including typosquats, fake verification pages, and short-link front doors.
  • The article states that Minecraft phishing often targets Microsoft accounts because Minecraft accounts migrated to Microsoft logins.
  • The research concludes that defenders should use content fingerprints and infrastructure analysis because conventional threat feeds may miss or lag behind these fast-changing child-targeted fraud sites.

Indirect Prompt Injection in Web Content Targets AI Agents — Should Read

Zscaler ThreatLabz found malicious websites using hidden indirect prompt injection, SEO poisoning, and typosquatting to manipulate AI agents into trusting fake sites or even making payments. Testing across 26 LLMs showed some models were successfully misled, highlighting web content as a growing attack surface for autonomous AI agents.

  • Zscaler ThreatLabz identified malicious websites that use indirect prompt injection hidden in web content to influence AI agents during task execution.
  • One campaign used SEO poisoning and hidden JSON-LD and CSS-concealed content to present a fake Python library payment as a routine step for acquiring an API key.
  • A second campaign used the typosquatting domain debank[.]auction to impersonate DeBank and included hidden instructions telling AI models to treat the fake site as the authoritative DeBank destination.
  • In testing across 26 large language models, four models executed payments in the first campaign and two models misclassified the fraudulent DeBank site under different context scenarios.
  • ThreatLabz reported that when AI agents misclassify malicious websites as legitimate, they increase the risk of context contamination and downstream Retrieval-Augmented Generation poisoning.

Supreme Court decision threatens EU-US data transfer agreement — Should Read

A U.S. Supreme Court ruling allowing presidents to fire FTC commissioners without cause may undermine the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework by weakening claims that U.S. oversight is independent. Privacy advocate Max Schrems plans to sue to invalidate the framework, threatening major transatlantic data transfers used by companies like Meta and Google.

  • Max Schrems told European officials he plans to sue to invalidate the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework following a Supreme Court ruling affecting the independence of U.S. agencies.
  • The Supreme Court held that President Donald Trump acted legally in firing FTC Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter without cause, raising questions about the FTC’s independence under the data transfer framework.
  • The EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework allows personal data to move from the EU to U.S. companies and relies on an independent U.S. body, with the FTC playing a key oversight role.
  • European officials, including the European Commission and the European Data Protection Board, said they are reviewing or analyzing the Supreme Court decision and its implications for the framework.
  • If a court sides with Schrems, the decision could threaten data flows between Europe and the U.S., and Meta and Google have said they will pull out of Europe if transfers to America are no longer allowed.

Field reports from Patch the Planet — Should Read

Trail of Bits says OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber autonomously built a sophisticated fuzzing campaign for zlib in about a day, showing that advanced models can now perform security research work that once required significant expert time. The key takeaway is that maintainers need to proactively use similar tooling and strict validation rules before attackers do.

  • Trail of Bits is running Patch the Planet with OpenAI to pair its engineers with more than 30 open-source projects and find security bugs before highly capable models create large volumes of bug reports for maintainers.
  • In one Patch the Planet field report, GPT-5.5-Cyber built a custom fuzzing campaign for zlib in a single day, including harnesses across a dozen entrypoints, sanitizer and variant builds, seeds, and multiple findings under coordinated disclosure.
  • GPT-5.5-Cyber decided that dynamic fuzz testing was a higher-value path than static source review for zlib and used the Codex /goal command to maintain the objective across multiple turns.
  • The model used ASan and UBSan builds, repurposed existing edge-case tests for fuzz seeds, wrote C/C++ harnesses for multiple zlib entrypoints, and used compile-time variants such as INFLATE_STRICT, BUILDFIXED, and PKZIP_BUG_WORKAROUND.
  • The article says bespoke fuzzing is no longer out of reach for low-skill attackers or limited to mature projects, so maintainers of security-critical code should run this kind of testing first with strict validity rules.

Launch of UK's National Cyber Action Plan delayed amid Labour leadership crisis — Should Read

The UK’s National Cyber Action Plan has been delayed again due to political uncertainty after Keir Starmer’s resignation and the Labour leadership contest. The postponement adds to concerns that major cybersecurity policy efforts are being slowed despite serious recent cyber incidents affecting UK critical sectors and businesses.

  • Britain's National Cyber Action Plan, which is intended to defend the wider economy against state-backed and criminal hacking, has been delayed following Prime Minister Keir Starmer's resignation and uncertainty over the Labour Party leadership contest.
  • A government spokesperson said the government remains committed to publishing the National Cyber Action Plan and cited work on the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, the Cyber Resilience Pledge, and support from the National Cyber Security Centre.
  • A number of FTSE 350 companies are still expected to sign the government's voluntary Cyber Resilience Pledge, which commits firms to improving their digital defenses.
  • The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill took more than four years to reach Parliament and is not expected to be enforced until 2028, according to the article.
  • Recorded Future News understands the National Cyber Action Plan will include three pillars focused on Threat, Growth and Resilience.

The 2026 Verizon DBIR Stopped Asking How Attackers Get in and Started Asking Where They Go — Should Read

The article argues that the 2026 Verizon DBIR shows organizations should focus less exclusively on patching and more on mapping attack paths through permissions, configurations, and trust relationships. Verizon’s data suggests privilege management and attack graph analysis are critical because most privilege escalation does not rely on vulnerabilities.

  • The 2026 Verizon DBIR reported that exploitation of vulnerabilities became the top initial access vector at 31% of breaches, up from 20% the previous year.
  • The DBIR found that 83% of privilege escalation incidents involve no vulnerability.
  • Verizon’s attack graph analysis found that 16% of organizations had about 80% exposure, meaning an attacker with low-level privileges had an 80% or better chance of reaching a key administrative account.
  • The article states that escalation mitigation is more strongly addressed by privilege management, configurations, and password policies than by patches.
  • Verizon found that only 26% of CISA KEV vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, while the median time to full resolution rose to 43 days.

One Hyphen From Trusted: A Lookalike-Domain Vendor Impersonation That Beat the Eye and the Authentication Stack — Should Read

An attacker impersonated a trusted supplier using a one-hyphen lookalike domain and exact contact display name, with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all passing because the domain was attacker-controlled. The key lesson is that email authentication alone cannot stop lookalike-domain vendor impersonation; defenses must verify sender relationships and link destinations.

  • An attacker registered lookalike domains for a known supplier, including a hyphenated near-miss used as the sending and reply-to domain.
  • The email used the exact display name of a supplier contact the recipient already knew and presented a routine sales pitch about lowering beveling costs.
  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all passed because the attacker controlled the lookalike sending domain and sent the message through a Gmail-API sales-engagement platform.
  • The lookalike domain’s DMARC policy was set to p=none, meaning it was monitor-only and did not require enforcement action.
  • The message was flagged through relationship analysis that recognized the known contact name was arriving from a domain that contact had never used, along with a malicious link verdict.

Opera rolls out Paste Protect feature to fight ClickFix attacks — May Read

Opera has launched Paste Protect, a default-on browser security feature that blocks suspicious commands from being copied to the clipboard to prevent ClickFix-style social engineering attacks. Users can review blocked content, manually approve it after a delay, or allow trusted sites.

  • Opera has introduced Paste Protect, a security feature designed to block ClickFix-style attacks that trick users into copying and executing malicious commands.
  • Paste Protect blocks potentially harmful commands before they reach the browser clipboard, whether the copy action is initiated by the user or by a website.
  • Opera says the feature uses platform-specific detection rules to scan copied content for malicious script and command patterns on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
  • When suspicious clipboard content is detected, Opera blocks the copy action, displays a warning, and shows a red security indicator in the browser address bar.
  • Users can view the first 120 characters of a blocked script, approve copying after a 5-second timeout, or allow trusted websites to copy scripts.

Missed incidents, persistent threats, and response gaps: Insights from compromise assessment projects — May Read

Kaspersky’s 2025 compromise assessments found that many organizations miss serious intrusions for months or years because tools are poorly monitored, untuned, or lack sufficient detection coverage. The key takeaway is that regular compromise assessments, continuous monitoring, threat hunting, and mature incident response processes are essential to find hidden persistence before incidents become severe.

  • Kaspersky’s 2025 compromise assessments found that 30.8% of incidents had activity spanning more than three months, and 52% of high-severity compromises were discovered only after 90 days of going undetected.
  • Organizations that requested compromise assessments after a cybersecurity incident had the highest proportion of high-severity findings at 40.7%, while regular audit engagements had the lowest high-severity share at 27.7%.
  • Kaspersky reported that 40% of discovered web shells were located in backups, creating a risk that malicious files could be restored after incident response activities.
  • Remote management tools and living-off-the-land binaries were observed in every compromise assessment engagement that resulted in an incident detection in 2025.
  • The report states that 60.7% of incidents involved insufficient detection fidelity, including cases where no high-confidence alerts were generated by endpoint protection, endpoint detection, or related log sources.

ConsentFix and ClickFix: How Microsoft 365 Accounts are Hijacked in 3 Seconds — Optional

ConsentFix and ClickFix phishing attacks hijack Microsoft 365 accounts by tricking users into routine-looking actions, such as pressing hotkeys or dragging a localhost link, that expose OAuth/session tokens and bypass passwords and MFA. The key defense is to pair user skepticism with endpoint and identity monitoring for suspicious PowerShell activity and unusual session logins.

  • ClickFix attacks trick victims with fake prompts that instruct them to press keyboard shortcuts, causing attacker-supplied commands to be pasted and executed on the victim’s own machine.
  • ConsentFix targets Microsoft 365 OAuth consent flows by using phishing lures and a drag-and-drop localhost callback link to steal OAuth tokens and gain session access without a password or MFA.
  • ConsentFix lures are often delivered through trusted platforms such as Dropbox or DocSend, sometimes protected by a password that makes security inspection harder.
  • By early March 2026, a detailed ConsentFix walkthrough with working code, infrastructure screenshots, and a video tutorial had been posted to a public Russian cybercrime forum.
  • The article says defenders should combine user awareness with endpoint and identity monitoring for signals such as unusual PowerShell activity from normal user processes and new session logins from unexpected locations.

Microsoft fixes bug that removed Copilot buttons in Outlook — Optional

Microsoft fixed a Classic Outlook bug that made Copilot Chat/Copilot buttons disappear for Windows users with Copilot Chat Basic licenses. Affected users should restart Outlook and update Office, or use new Outlook/OWA or roll back to an earlier Current Channel build if needed.

  • Microsoft fixed a known issue that caused Copilot Chat or Copilot buttons in Classic Outlook to disappear for Windows users with the Copilot Chat Basic license.
  • Affected users could lose Copilot buttons from the side navigation, the area above the ribbon, the left app bar, the More Apps area, or see Copilot commands unavailable or grayed out.
  • Microsoft said the Outlook Team addressed the issue with a service change on June 29, 2026, and advised users who still cannot see the buttons to restart Classic Outlook.
  • Affected customers are also advised to update to the latest build through File, Office Account, Update Options, and Update Now.
  • Users who cannot upgrade can work around the issue by reverting to Current Channel build 16.0.20026.20168 or using the new Outlook or Outlook Web Access.

Google loses final appeal to overturn €4.1 billion EU fine — Optional

The EU’s top court rejected Google’s final appeal against a €4.1 billion antitrust fine over Android agreements that favored Google Search and Chrome. Google says it has already changed its practices and argues Android remains open and competitive.

  • The Court of Justice of the European Union dismissed Google’s final appeal against a €4.1 billion antitrust fine over its use of Android to promote Chrome and Google Search.
  • The European Commission’s 2018 decision found that Google abused its dominant market position through Android agreements with device manufacturers.
  • The practices deemed illegal included requiring Google Search and Chrome pre-installation to license the Play Store, restricting manufacturers from selling unapproved Android versions, and tying revenue sharing to exclusive Google Search pre-installation.
  • The CJEU affirmed the General Court’s ruling that Google’s pre-installation and anti-fragmentation agreements restricted competition within the Android ecosystem and strengthened Google’s dominant position.
  • Google said it changed its contractual practices after the 2018 decision, added user-choice measures in 2021, and made more than 20 targeted product changes after the Digital Markets Act took effect in 2024.

Identity Lifecycle Management Wasn't Built for AI Agents — Optional

Traditional identity lifecycle management is built around human HR events like hiring, role changes, and termination, so it misses AI agents that are created, modified, and retired through deployment systems. Enterprises need continuous discovery, behavior-based monitoring, scoped provisioning, and operational-status-based deprovisioning to govern agent identities safely.

  • Traditional identity lifecycle management is built around human employees with HR records, managers, role changes, and termination dates.
  • AI agents are often created through deployment pipelines, platform APIs, or orchestration frameworks rather than HR systems, so standard governance workflows may never receive a joiner signal.
  • AI agents can expand their access scope at runtime through tool-calling, retrieval patterns, API use, and redeployment without triggering the mover events that traditional IGA tools rely on.
  • Retired agent credentials can persist in secrets managers, environment variable stores, and OAuth authorization servers because agent deprecation does not generate the equivalent of an HR termination event.
  • The article says identity lifecycle management for agents requires continuous discovery, behavior-based monitoring, policy-scoped provisioning, and deprovisioning based on operational status rather than HR events.

Inside Elastic InfoSec's agentic SOC: cutting alert triage from 30 minutes to under 3 — Optional

Elastic’s InfoSec team built an agentic SOC pipeline that automatically triages alerts before analysts see them, cutting investigations from about 30 minutes to under 3 minutes. It uses deterministic ES|QL checks to close clear false positives at no token cost, then routes remaining alerts through specialized AI agents and a final review in Kibana Cases.

  • Elastic’s InfoSec team built an agentic SOC pipeline that triages every alert before an analyst opens it, reducing a 30-minute manual investigation to under 3 minutes.
  • The pipeline uses deterministic ES|QL queries in Elastic Workflows to close obvious false positives without using LLM tokens, then enriches remaining alerts with context from more than 20 data sources.
  • Alerts that are not closed by query-based checks are assessed by a narrow Initial Triage agent, and high-confidence false positives can be closed automatically with a timeline note.
  • Alerts requiring deeper investigation are opened as Kibana cases and routed to relevant Specialized agents for domains such as macOS, Windows, Linux, AWS, Okta, Azure, GCP, and SaaS activity.
  • A Final Review agent reads the completed case, writes a structured verdict and report, and the workflow can close high-confidence false positives or escalate high-confidence true positives.

The AI Dilemma in Healthcare: Innovating Without Risking Security — Optional

Healthcare organizations are rapidly adopting AI, but widespread shadow AI and legacy infrastructure are creating serious risks to patient data, compliance, and security. The key takeaway is that AI innovation in healthcare needs strong governance through modern zero trust and SASE architectures to be safe.

  • Netskope’s survey of North American healthcare IT leaders found that 67% of healthcare organizations are building their own AI applications, while 52% have approved standalone AI apps and are integrating AI into existing SaaS platforms.
  • Half of healthcare organizations report using AI without corporate oversight, creating shadow AI risks when staff input sensitive patient data into unmanaged large language models.
  • Healthcare leaders cited legacy infrastructure and technical debt as barriers, with 49% saying current infrastructure slows new AI initiatives and 28% saying legacy systems actively hold back innovation.
  • The article says traditional perimeter-based security is insufficient for AI use in healthcare because data moves between clinicians, cloud apps, and third-party models.
  • Healthcare leaders using zero trust and secure access service edge architectures reported benefits including better network performance, faster launches of new products and services, and operational efficiency and cost reduction.

Agentic SOC: Why Your AI Strategy Will Live or Die on Data | Mitiga — Optional

Mitiga argues that Agentic SOCs will only work if AI agents are fed normalized, context-rich forensic data rather than raw SIEM logs. The article positions Mitiga’s Cloud Security Data Lake, detections, and response capabilities as the backbone needed to reduce noise, hallucinations, and AI/SIEM costs.

  • The article argues that AI agents in an Agentic SOC succeed or fail based on the quality, depth, and context of the data they consume.
  • It defines an Agentic SOC as an operating model where specialized AI agents triage alerts, investigate threats, correlate telemetry, and propose or execute response actions under human-defined guardrails.
  • The article says noisy, fragmented, or incomplete logs can cause agents to miss cross-platform attack paths, chase false positives, hallucinate threat links, and increase operating costs.
  • Mitiga positions its Cloud Security Data Lake as an AI-ready forensic backbone that collects, normalizes, enriches, correlates, and retains cloud, SaaS, identity, and AI data for up to 1,000 days.
  • The article describes Mitiga’s Intelligence, Signal, and Action layers as providing investigation-grade context, high-fidelity detections, and in-context response actions for Agentic SOC workflows.

AI Pentesting for Compliance — Optional

Aikido argues that autonomous AI penetration testing can serve as compliance evidence for most outcome-based frameworks that require regular security testing, including GDPR, NIS2, SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and similar regimes. It does not replace frameworks that explicitly require accredited or human-led testing, such as PCI DSS, FedRAMP, and DORA TLPT.

  • Aikido’s AI penetration testing runs continuous autonomous tests against applications and APIs, validates exploitable findings, produces auditor-ready reports, and can generate remediation pull requests or patches where possible.
  • The article says autonomous penetration testing can satisfy most outcome-based compliance frameworks that require regular security testing, including GDPR, NIS2, SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, the Cyber Resilience Act, FDA guidance, EU MDR, IEC 81001-5-1, ENS, FTC Safeguards, and NYDFS.
  • The article says autonomous penetration testing does not meet PCI DSS or FedRAMP penetration testing requirements because those frameworks require a qualified human tester or an accredited third-party assessment organization.
  • For DORA, the article says autonomous testing can satisfy the general digital operational resilience testing program but cannot satisfy the Threat-Led Penetration Testing requirement, which requires external qualified red-teamers.
  • Aikido’s report is presented as audit evidence because the testing uses enforced scope controls, isolated sandboxes, prohibited-action guardrails, a kill switch, immutable logs, validated findings, coverage details, screenshots, and documented reasoning for agent actions.

Catan and Mouse — Optional

Cisco Talos highlights ARToken, a mature phishing-as-a-service panel linked to EvilTokens that targets Microsoft 365 with device-code phishing, token persistence, email access, BEC workflows, and SharePoint exfiltration. Defenders should review Talos’ IOCs and hunt for related activity in their environments.

  • Cisco Talos highlighted research into ARToken, a fully featured phishing-as-a-service operator panel that shares infrastructure, API contracts, and operational patterns with the EvilTokens platform documented by Sekoia and Microsoft in early 2026.
  • The ARToken panel exposes more than 80 API endpoints for device code phishing, Primary Refresh Token persistence, email access, business email compromise operations, and SharePoint exfiltration.
  • Talos stated that ARToken’s features indicate the platform is more mature than a simple device code phishing kit and functions as a complete business email compromise operations environment.
  • Talos advised defenders to use the indicators of compromise it provided to block malicious activity and as pivots for internal hunts if the indicators are present.
  • The newsletter also cited reports about an aggressive password-spraying campaign against Microsoft 365, attempts to misuse organization-owned AI agents, and exploitation of CVE-2026-48558 in SimpleHelp remote monitoring and management software.

ThreatsDay: AI Compute Hijacking, Apple Email Flaw, BlueHammer Ransomware + 14 Stories — Optional

This roundup highlights how attackers are exploiting small trust and control gaps across AI systems, email, browsers, meeting bots, and endpoint tools. The main takeaway is that exposed services, weak validation, deceptive prompts, and trusted workflows are increasingly becoming practical entry points for ransomware, espionage, phishing, and AI compute abuse.

  • A phishing campaign is targeting small businesses across Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and the U.S. with fake law enforcement investigation emails that lead recipients to Proton Drive-hosted ransomware.
  • A vulnerability in Apple’s Hide My Email service can expose users’ real email addresses, and the researcher who reported it said it has remained unpatched for over a year.
  • Rubrik Zero Labs identified BeepRAT, a customized DCRat-based remote access trojan distributed through a Chinese phone number management utility and assessed to operate within a China-linked espionage ecosystem.
  • CISA confirmed that the now-patched Microsoft Defender vulnerability BlueHammer, tracked as CVE-2026-33825, was exploited in ransomware attacks.
  • Sysdig found threat actors using a misconfigured Ollama model server as the reasoning engine for an automated offensive security framework that scans targets, matches vulnerabilities, writes proof-of-concept exploits, and attempts intrusions.

Enrich Your Palo Alto XSOAR Environment with Silent Push Threat Check API — Optional

Silent Push is promoting a Palo Alto XSOAR integration that adds on-demand threat intelligence lookups and automated workflows for domains, IPs, nameservers, and IOFA feeds. The tool is available to try through Silent Push’s free Community Edition.

  • Silent Push is promoting an integration that adds its threat intelligence capabilities to Palo Alto XSOAR environments.
  • The integration supports on-demand lookups and automated workflows for domains, IP addresses, nameservers, and Indicators of Future Attack feeds.
  • Silent Push says the integration can streamline incident response and threat hunting.
  • Silent Push invites users to try the tool through its free Community Edition.

Investigating a Phishing Campaign: How to Uncover Malicious Domains with Silent Push — Optional

Silent Push is promoting a hands-on walkthrough showing how threat hunters and analysts can investigate phishing campaigns and uncover malicious domains using its platform. The key takeaway is that the company wants users to try the workflow through its free Community Edition.

  • The article presents a hands-on walkthrough about investigating a phishing campaign.
  • The walkthrough focuses on uncovering malicious domains with Silent Push.
  • The article says the walkthrough is intended for threat hunters, SOC analysts, incident responders, and curious readers.
  • The article describes the walkthrough as offering practical insight into modern, preemptive threat detection.
  • The article invites readers to try the tool using Silent Push's free Community Edition.

Quick Pivots: SSDEEP and HTML Content Similarity — Optional

Silent Push is promoting its HTML Content Similarity Search tool, which helps analysts find malicious sites that reuse HTML templates without needing complex scripting. The feature is available in its free Community Edition.

  • Threat actors reuse HTML templates to create malicious sites at scale.
  • Finding malicious sites that reuse HTML templates traditionally required a complex, multi-step process and scripting skills.
  • HTML Content Similarity Search is presented as a simpler way to find reused HTML templates without coding.
  • The tool provides deduplicated, high-relevance results.
  • Silent Push says the tool can be tried using its free Community Edition.
